title: I spent weeks trying to make AI-generated isometric assets work. I eventually switched to 3D.
author: Kiko_Production
selftext:
I've been building a city builder and originally planned to make almost the entire world from generated 2D isometric assets.

It sounded like the easier option.

Fixed camera, generated buildings, normal maps for lighting, a few variations for each asset, done.

In practice, maintaining consistency became one of the most annoying parts of development.

Even with references, fixed angles and rough base shapes, generation kept introducing small differences in perspective, proportions and geometry. One building could look completely fine on its own, but once I started putting a city together, those differences became much more obvious.

Normal maps were probably the point where I started questioning the whole pipeline. I could make them work, but every new asset meant another round of fixing something that would just exist naturally in 3D.

So I started rebuilding the environment in actual 3D.

This video is a very early test. Most assets are placeholders, NPC behavior is unfinished, there are way too many residents spawned here, and there is a lot of dev garbage still visible.

But this was probably the first test where I really understood why I want to keep going in this direction.

I can throw a ridiculous number of residents into the town, move the camera around them, zoom all the way out, change the environment, lighting or animation without having to regenerate another version of every asset.

And more importantly, the city suddenly feels like an actual place rather than a collection of isometric images.

I'm still keeping the stylized look, 2D character art and UI. I'm not trying to turn it into a realistic 3D game.

Ironically, I switched to 3D because I thought it would be harder, and so far a lot of the production problems have actually become simpler.

It's still way too early to say whether that will remain true once the project gets larger, but right now I'm pretty happy I made the switch.

replies.author: Kiko_Production
replies.body:
I start with a style bible I put together while the game was still 2D. I generate a building concept based on it and check how it reads from a distance. Once the design looks right, I generate four matching views: front, back, left, and right.

Those go into Tripo for the 3D model and textures. Then I use Astra or Sonnet 5.5 to help clean it up in Blender patch holes, fix geometry, remove texture artifacts, and adjust the scale before testing it in-game.

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
...Have you tried anything more complex? 

All of the methods I've tried for 3D are able to handle simple objects, but when it comes to stuff like, say, fantasy creatures... the end results are completely awful.

comments.author: worldbefree83
comments.body: Extremely curious as to your workflow. Impressive results

replies.author: Kiko_Production
replies.body:
Thanks! A lot of the consistency comes from a style bible I made during the original 2D version, covering the buildings’ look, proportions, and layout.  
For the 3D version, I generate a concept first, then four views of the same design and use those as references in Tripo. After generating the model and textures, I use GPT-6 Astra or Sonnet 5.5 to help with cleanup in Blender. Finally, I compare it with the existing buildings under the game’s lighting and make another pass on anything that doesn’t fit.

comments.author: liatris4405
comments.body: Yeah, I understand because I was also trying to make a game with pixel art. The truth is, current generative AI still isn't very good at pixel art. It's actually much easier to move development forward in 3D.
